questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A child of mass m sits on a car seat which is accelerating horizontally at 0.50 g (where g is the acceleration of free fall).

What is the magnitude of the total force F exerted by the car seat on the child?
questions.stemText: A child of mass m sits on a car seat which is accelerating horizontally at 0.50 g (where g is the acceleration of free fall). F What is the magnitude of the total force F exerted by the car seat on the child? A 0.50 mg B 1.0 mg C 1.1 mg D 1.5 mg

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires seeing that the seat supplies both the vertical support and the horizontal accelerating force, then combining vectors.
questions.misconception: Taking only the horizontal or only the vertical component of the contact force

explanation.body:
For vertical equilibrium, $F_y = mg$. For horizontal motion, $F_x = ma = 0.50\,mg$.

$F = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2} = \sqrt{(0.50mg)^2 + (mg)^2} = 1.1\,mg$.

perOption.A: Only the horizontal component $F_x$; ignores supporting the weight.
perOption.B: Only the vertical component $F_y$; ignores the acceleration.
perOption.C: Correct. Vector sum of the two perpendicular components.
perOption.D: Adds the components as scalars instead of as vectors.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two blocks of identical size, one made of wood and the other of copper, are at rest on the ground as shown in (1) and (2). Both blocks are then accelerated upwards by an applied force F as shown in (3).

Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.stemText: Two blocks of identical size, one made of wood and the other of copper, are at rest on the ground as shown in (1) and (2). Both blocks are then accelerated upwards by an applied force F as shown in (3). (3) (1) (2) copper wood wood copper copper wood force F ground ground ground Which of the following statements is correct? A The force by ground on the copper block in (1) is greater than the force by the ground on the wooden block in (2) because the copper block is denser than the wooden block and exerts a bigger force on the ground. B The force by the wooden block on the copper block in (1) is the same as that by the copper block on the wooden block in (2) due to Newton’s Third Law. C The force by the copper block on the wooden block in (3) is equal to that by the copper block on the wooden block in (2). D The applied force F on the wooden block in (3) is greater than the force by the ground on the copper block in (1).

options.label: A
options.text: The force by ground on the copper block in (1) is greater than the force by the ground on the wooden block in (2) because the copper block is denser than the wooden block and exerts a bigger force on the ground.

options.label: B
options.text: The force by the wooden block on the copper block in (1) is the same as that by the copper block on the wooden block in (2) due to Newton’s Third Law.

options.label: C
options.text: The force by the copper block on the wooden block in (3) is equal to that by the copper block on the wooden block in (2).

options.label: D
options.text: The applied force F on the wooden block in (3) is greater than the force by the ground on the copper block in (1).

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires careful free-body reasoning for stacked blocks at rest and accelerating, and correct identification of third-law pairs.
questions.misconception: Misidentifying Newton's third-law pairs and ignoring that acceleration changes contact forces

explanation.body: Treat the two blocks as one system. At rest, the ground’s upward force balances their combined weight. When the system accelerates upward in (3), the applied force must exceed that combined weight.

perOption.A: The ground supports the same combined weight in (1) and (2).
perOption.B: The third-law partner is the copper block’s force on the wooden block in (1), in the same configuration.
perOption.C: In (3), the wood’s upward force on the copper must exceed the copper’s weight, so the copper pushes down harder on the wood than in (2).
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A body is initially at rest on a horizontal frictionless table.

A force then acts on it that varies with time as shown.

Which graph represents the variation with time of the velocity of the body?
questions.stemText: A body is initially at rest on a horizontal frictionless table. A force then acts on it that varies with time as shown. force 0 0 time Which graph represents the variation with time of the velocity of the body? A velocity 0 0 time B velocity 0 0 time C velocity 0 0 time D velocity 0 0 time

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct link between constant force, constant acceleration and a linear velocity rise.
questions.misconception: Thinking velocity follows the force, or that the body stops when the force is removed

explanation.body: By $F_{\mathrm{net}}=ma$, the constant positive force produces constant acceleration, so velocity increases along a straight line. When the net force is zero, acceleration is zero and the velocity–time graph is horizontal.

perOption.A: Copies the force pulse and shows instantaneous changes in velocity.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Shows deceleration after the force has dropped to zero.
perOption.D: Shows increasing acceleration during a constant force.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A lorry is pulling a cart of mass 600 kg with a rope at a constant speed along a straight horizontal road. The horizontal force resisting the motion of the cart is 40 N.

The lorry now accelerates at 0.15 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$.

What is the tension in the rope?
questions.stemText: A lorry is pulling a cart of mass 600 kg with a rope at a constant speed along a straight horizontal road. The horizontal force resisting the motion of the cart is 40 N. The lorry now accelerates at 0.15 m s-2. What is the tension in the rope? A 65 N B 100 N C 130 N D 195 N

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: One application of F = ma with resistive force included.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the resistive force or using only ma

explanation.body: The cart has a forward tension $T$ and a backward resistive force of $40\ \mathrm N$. Newton's second law gives $T-40=600(0.15)$, so $T=130\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.A: A tension of $65\ \mathrm N$ leaves only $25\ \mathrm N$ to accelerate the cart.
perOption.B: A tension of $100\ \mathrm N$ leaves only $60\ \mathrm N$ of net force.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: A tension of $195\ \mathrm N$ gives $155\ \mathrm N$ of net force, exceeding the required $90\ \mathrm N$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: The motions of two objects X and Y along a straight line are shown in the following velocity-time graphs. [Graph X: velocity falls linearly from $v$ at $t=0$ to 0 at $t_1$, then rises linearly to $v$ at $t_2$. Graph Y: velocity falls linearly from $3v/4$ at $t=0$ to $-v/4$ at $t_1$, then rises linearly to $3v/4$ at $t_2$.] How do the magnitudes of the displacement and the total distance travelled compare for the two objects from time 0 to time $t_2$? (displacement, distance) A different, different B different, same C same, different D same, same

stemImage.alt: Question 2: The motions of two objects X and Y along a straight line are shown in the following velocity- time graphs. − How do the magnitudes of the displacement and the t

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising that shifting the graph down changes both net area and absolute area.
questions.misconception: Assuming distance is unchanged because the graph shapes are identical

explanation.body: Displacement is the area above the time axis minus the area below it. For X both triangles lie above the axis, while the negative area for Y partly cancels its positive area, so Y has the smaller displacement. Distance adds the magnitudes of the areas on both sides of the axis. Y has a lower positive peak ($3v/4$ versus $v$), and even after including its negative portion as a positive area, its total distance is smaller than X’s.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Adding the magnitude of Y’s negative area still leaves Y with less total distance.
perOption.C: Subtracting Y’s negative-area magnitude gives a smaller displacement than X’s.
perOption.D: Both Y’s signed area and its total unsigned area are smaller than X’s.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: The diagram shows a man standing in a lift. The forces acting on the man and the forces acting on the lift are shown below. [Diagram: man with N upward and $W_1$ downward; lift with T upward, $W_2$ and D downward.] N is the force from the lift floor on the man. $W_1$ is the weight of the man. T is the tension in the lift cable. $W_2$ is the weight of the lift. D is the force from the man on the lift floor. Which of the following statements is correct? A $(W_1 + W_2)$ is always equal to T. B If $N = W_1$, the lift must be at rest. C N and $W_1$ are always equal and opposite. D If $T = (D + W_2)$, the lift must have a constant velocity.

stemImage.alt: Question 4: The diagram shows a man standing in a lift. The forces acting on the man and the forces acting on the lift are shown below. Which of the following statements is

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs careful free-body analysis of separate bodies and Newton's laws.
questions.misconception: Equating zero resultant force with being at rest

explanation.body: Applying Newton’s second law to the lift gives $T-W_2-D=m_{\mathrm{lift}}a$. If $T=D+W_2$, the resultant is zero, so $a=0$ and the lift has constant velocity, including the possibility of rest.

perOption.A: The cable tension equals the combined weight only when the lift system has zero acceleration.
perOption.B: Equal forces on the man imply zero acceleration, which also allows motion at constant nonzero velocity.
perOption.C: Both forces act on the man, and their magnitudes can differ when he accelerates.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A trolley runs down a slope with a constant acceleration a. The mass of the trolley is now doubled, and the trolley is allowed to run down the same slope. In both cases effects of friction and air resistance are negligible. A The accelerating force is the same. B The acceleration is $\frac{1}{2}a$. C The acceleration is a. D The acceleration is 2a.

stemImage.alt: Question 5: A trolley runs down a slope with a constant acceleration a. The mass of the trolley is now doubled, and the trolley is allowed to run down the same slope. In bo

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Standard result that acceleration down a frictionless slope is independent of mass.
questions.misconception: Thinking heavier objects accelerate differently

explanation.body: The downhill component of weight is $F=mg\sin\theta$, so $a=F/m=g\sin\theta$. With double the mass, the downhill force doubles to $F'=2mg\sin\theta$. Dividing by the new mass gives $a'=F'/(2m)=g\sin\theta=a$.

perOption.A: The downhill component of weight doubles when the mass doubles.
perOption.B: Assumes the downhill force stays fixed as the mass doubles.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Doubles the force but overlooks the doubling of the mass.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A force of 54 N pushes two touching blocks of mass 6.0 kg and 2.0 kg along a flat surface. The frictional force between the blocks and the surface is 6.0 N.

What is the force exerted on the 2.0 kg block?
questions.stemText: A force of 54 N pushes two touching blocks of mass 6.0 kg and 2.0 kg along a flat surface. The frictional force between the blocks and the surface is 6.0 N. What is the force exerted on the 2.0 kg block? A 12 N B 36 N C 45 N D 48 N

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Whole-system acceleration then Newton's second law on one block.
questions.misconception: Taking the force on the 2.0 kg block as the applied force minus friction

explanation.body: For the two blocks together, the net force is $54-6.0=48\ \mathrm{N}$, so their common acceleration is $48/8.0=6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Applying Newton’s second law to the $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block gives a resultant horizontal force of $2.0(6.0)=12\ \mathrm{N}$. This is also the contact force if the friction shown acts entirely on the larger block, as assumed in the key.

perOption.A: Correct. This is the resultant force on the smaller block.
perOption.B: Uses the mass of the larger block with the common acceleration.
perOption.C: Uses the wrong system or force balance for the smaller block, whose resultant is 12 N.
perOption.D: Uses the resultant force on both blocks combined.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The graph shows how the velocity v of an object moving in a straight line varies with time t from t = 0 to t = T.

Which statement is correct?
questions.stemText: The graph shows how the velocity v of an object moving in a straight line varies with time t from t = 0 to t = T. Which statement is correct? A The displacement is greatest when the velocity is zero. B The object changes direction when the acceleration is zero. C The displacement increases only when the acceleration is positive. D The speed is greatest when the acceleration is zero.

options.label: A
options.text: The displacement is greatest when the velocity is zero.

options.label: B
options.text: The object changes direction when the acceleration is zero.

options.label: C
options.text: The displacement increases only when the acceleration is positive.

options.label: D
options.text: The speed is greatest when the acceleration is zero.

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires reading gradient and sign of a v–t graph rather than any calculation.
questions.misconception: Confusing zero acceleration with change of direction

explanation.body: The maximum speed occurs at a peak or trough of the velocity–time graph, where $a=dv/dt=0$. Direction changes when velocity changes sign, and displacement increases wherever velocity is positive.

perOption.A: At $t=T$ the velocity is zero and the displacement has returned to zero, although the interior zero crossing does coincide with maximum displacement.
perOption.B: Direction changes when $v$ changes sign, while $a=0$ at the velocity extrema.
perOption.C: Displacement increases whenever $v>0$, even if the acceleration is negative.
perOption.D: Correct. The greatest speed occurs at a horizontal tangent.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A hot air balloon of total mass M is descending vertically with a constant acceleration of 2.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. For the hot air balloon to ascend with an upward acceleration of 4.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$, some mass needs to be removed.

Assuming the upward lift remains the same, what is the amount of mass that must be removed?
questions.stemText: A hot air balloon of total mass M is descending vertically with a constant acceleration of 2.0 m s–2. For the hot air balloon to ascend with an upward acceleration of 4.0 m s–2, some mass needs to be removed. Assuming the upward lift remains the same, what is the amount of mass that must be removed? A 0.14M B 0.43M C 0.57M D 0.86M

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Two applications of Newton's second law with a changing mass and careful sign handling.
questions.misconception: Ignoring direction of acceleration or forgetting the mass changes in the second case

explanation.body: Let $L$ be the lift. On descent, Newton’s second law gives $Mg-L=2M$, so $L=M(g-2)$. On ascent, for the remaining mass $M_1$, $L-M_1g=4M_1$, so $L=M_1(g+4)$. Equating the lifts gives $M_1=0.57M$, so the mass removed is $0.43M$.

perOption.A: Counts only the initial downward acceleration in the required change of acceleration.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gives the mass remaining after removal.
perOption.D: Overstates the mass reduction by doubling the required fraction.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A trolley of mass 0.50 kg moves with a certain acceleration down a runway which is inclined to the horizontal at $15^\circ$. If the angle of inclination is increased to $20^\circ$, the acceleration of the trolley would be doubled. What is the frictional force, assumed to be the same in both cases, acting on the trolley? A 0.12 N B 0.41 N C 0.86 N D 4.9 N

stemImage.alt: Question 4: A trolley of mass 0.50 kg moves with a certain acceleration down a runway which is inclined to the horizontal at 15. If the angle of inclination is increased t

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs two Newton's second law equations with the acceleration ratio, then solving simultaneously.
questions.misconception: Ignoring friction in one case or doubling the gravity component too

explanation.body: Along the runway at $15^\circ$, Newton’s second law gives $mg\sin15^\circ-f=ma$. At $20^\circ$, it gives $mg\sin20^\circ-f=2ma$. Doubling the first equation and subtracting the second eliminates $a$, giving $f=mg(2\sin15^\circ-\sin20^\circ)=0.86\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.A: This friction is too small to make the second net force twice the first.
perOption.B: This is the increase in the downhill component of weight, which equals $ma$ for the first incline.
perOption.C: Correct. This friction satisfies both force equations.
perOption.D: This is the trolley’s full weight and would exceed the downhill component on both inclines.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Two small masses A and B are placed at the bottom and top of a smooth slope inclined at $30.0^\circ$ to the horizontal. At time $t = 0$, mass A is launched up the slope with an initial speed of $4.00\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ while mass B is released from rest at the top of the slope. The two masses collide at a point along the slope. [Diagram: right-angled slope at $30.0^\circ$, A at the bottom, B at the top] The length of the slope is $5.00\ \mathrm{m}$. At what time does the collision occur? A $0.681\ \mathrm{s}$ B $1.25\ \mathrm{s}$ C $1.50\ \mathrm{s}$ D $2.46\ \mathrm{s}$

stemImage.alt: Question 5: Two small masses A and B are placed at the top and bottom of a smooth slope inclined at 30.0 to the horizontal. At time t = 0, mass A is launched up the slope

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Best solved by noticing both masses share the same acceleration, so relative motion is uniform.
questions.misconception: Thinking the accelerations make the relative motion non-uniform

explanation.body: Let $a=g\sin30^\circ$ be the common downslope acceleration. At collision, A is $4t-\frac12at^2$ up from the bottom and B is $\frac12at^2$ down from the top. These displacements sum to $5.00\ \mathrm{m}$, so the acceleration terms cancel and $t=5.00/4.00=1.25\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Double-counts the effect of gravity on the closing motion by treating A as speeding up the slope.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses a time at which $4.00t=6.00\ \mathrm{m}$, greater than the initial separation.
perOption.D: Uses a time long enough for B to have already reached the bottom.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Identical beads are tied at various points on four equal length light inextensible strings. The strings are hung from the ceiling with the lowest bead just touching the floor. Each string is released at the top, so that the beads fall towards the floor. Air resistance is negligible.

When each bead hits the floor, a sound is produced.

Which of the following will result in sound produced at a constant time interval?
questions.stemText: Identical beads are tied at various points on four equal length light inextensible strings. The strings are hung from the ceiling with the lowest bead just touching the floor. Each string is released at the top, so that the beads fall towards the floor. Air resistance is negligible. When each bead hits the floor, a sound is produced. Which of the following will result in sound produced at a constant time interval? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs recognising that equal time intervals require heights in the ratio 1:4:9:16.
questions.misconception: Assuming equally spaced beads give equally spaced sounds

explanation.body: For a constant interval $T$, bead $n$ must fall for $nT$, so its starting height is $s=\frac12g(nT)^2$. The heights above the floor are therefore proportional to $0,1,4,9,16,\ldots$, as in D.

perOption.A: Spaces the beads more closely toward the ceiling, where the gaps need to be larger.
perOption.B: Uses equal height gaps, which give shorter time gaps at greater heights.
perOption.C: Increases the gaps but misses the square-number heights, starting with heights in the ratio $1:3$ instead of $1:4$.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A ball is held above the ground and released. It falls to the ground and bounces several times.

The graph shows the variation with time t of the velocity v of the ball.

Four points on the graph are labelled P, Q, R and S.

Which statement is not correct?
questions.stemText: A ball is held above the ground and released. It falls to the ground and bounces several times. The graph shows the variation with time t of the velocity v of the ball. v Q S P 0 t 0 R Four points on the graph are labelled P, Q, R and S. Which statement is not correct? A The area under line PQ represents the initial height of the ball. B The collisions of the ball with the ground are inelastic. C The gradient of the line RS represents the acceleration due to free fall. D The maximum upwards velocity of the ball is reached at point Q.

options.label: A
options.text: The area under line PQ represents the initial height of the ball.

options.label: B
options.text: The collisions of the ball with the ground are inelastic.

options.label: C
options.text: The gradient of the line RS represents the acceleration due to free fall.

options.label: D
options.text: The maximum upwards velocity of the ball is reached at point Q.

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must deduce the sign convention (downward positive) from the graph before judging each statement.
questions.misconception: Assuming upward is positive and so misreading which point is the maximum upward velocity

explanation.body: PQ describes the initial fall, so positive velocity on this graph is directed downwards. Q is the greatest downward velocity, while the greatest upward speed occurs at R immediately after the first bounce.

perOption.A: The area under PQ gives the downward displacement from release at P to first impact at Q.
perOption.B: The reduced speed after each impact shows a loss of kinetic energy in the collision.
perOption.C: The positive gradient of RS gives the downward acceleration of free fall.
perOption.D: Correct. Q is the point of maximum downward speed.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A camera drone of mass 1.20 kg hovers steadily above ground using four propellers. Each of the propellers pushes 0.50 kg of air vertically downward each second.

[Diagram: a quadcopter drone with four propellers on arms and a camera mounted underneath.]

Assume that the air above the propellers is stationary and that the drone remains level throughout.

What is the speed of the air leaving each propeller?

A $1.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$   B $2.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$   C $5.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$   D $24\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 4: A camera drone of mass 1.20 kg hovers steadily above ground using four propellers. Each of the propellers pushes 0.50 kg of air vertically downward each second.

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must link the thrust to the rate of change of momentum of the air and share the weight among four propellers.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to share the weight among the four propellers

explanation.body:
Since the drone hovers steadily and stays level, each propeller provides an equal share of the weight:

thrust per propeller $= \dfrac{1.20 \times 9.81}{4} = 2.943\ \mathrm{N}$

By Newton's second law, $F = \dfrac{dp}{dt} = \dfrac{m}{t}(v - 0)$, where $\dfrac{m}{t} = 0.50\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$ for each propeller:

$2.943 = 0.50\,v \Rightarrow v = 5.886 \approx 5.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

perOption.A: Gives the drone's mass value (1.2) rather than calculating a speed.
perOption.B: Takes the thrust per propeller (2.94 N) as the answer without dividing by the mass flow rate.
perOption.C: Correct. Thrust per propeller = (mass flow rate) $\times$ $v$.
perOption.D: Uses the drone's whole weight for one propeller instead of sharing it among four.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A car is travelling in a straight horizontal line at a constant speed of $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Rain falls vertically downwards and enters an open container fixed securely to the car at a constant rate of $0.50\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$. After entering the container, the rainwater moves horizontally with the car.

What is the horizontal force exerted by the container on the car as a result of collecting the rain?

A. $0\ \mathrm{N}$
B. $5.0\ \mathrm{N}$
C. $10\ \mathrm{N}$
D. $20\ \mathrm{N}$

stemImage.alt: Question 3: A car is travelling in a straight horizontal line at a constant speed of 20 m s−1. Rain falls vertically downwards and enters an open container fixed securely t

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires applying the momentum-rate form of Newton's second law to incoming rain at constant car speed.
questions.misconception: Assuming constant car speed means the collected rain requires no force

explanation.body: The collected rain gains horizontal momentum at the rate $F=\frac{d(mv)}{dt}=v\frac{dm}{dt}=(20)(0.50)=10\ \mathrm{N}$. The container therefore exerts a $10\ \mathrm{N}$ backward force on the car as the rain pushes back on it.

perOption.A: Ignores the horizontal momentum gained by the rain.
perOption.B: Underestimates the force by using less than the full horizontal velocity gain at the given mass flow rate.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Omits the factor of $0.50$ from the mass flow rate.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
X and Y are two objects on a frictionless table connected by a string. The mass of X is $2\ \mathrm{kg}$ and the mass of Y is $4\ \mathrm{kg}$. The mass of the string is negligible. A constant horizontal force of $12\ \mathrm{N}$ acts on Y.

[On a horizontal table, block X ($2\ \mathrm{kg}$) is to the left of block Y ($4\ \mathrm{kg}$). A horizontal string joins them, and a $12\ \mathrm{N}$ arrow points right from Y.]

What are the acceleration of Y and the magnitude of the tension in the string?

Acceleration of Y / $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, tension in the string / $\mathrm{N}$
A 2, 4
B 2, 6
C 3, 4
D 3, 6

stemImage.alt: Question 3: X and Y are two objects on a frictionless table connected by a string. The mass of X is 2 kg and the mass of Y is 4 kg. The mass of the string is negligible. A

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires applying Newton’s second law to the pair and then to one block.
questions.misconception: Applying the full pulling force to Y alone

explanation.body: For the two blocks together, $F_{\mathrm{net}}=ma$ gives $12=(4+2)a$, so $a=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. For X, the tension is the net horizontal force, so $T=2(2)=4\ \mathrm{N}$. Using Y gives the same result from $12-T=4(2)$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: The acceleration is right, but the tension is the force needed to accelerate the $2\ \mathrm{kg}$ block, giving $4\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.C: The tension is right, but dividing $12\ \mathrm{N}$ by Y’s mass alone ignores X.
perOption.D: Dividing by Y’s mass alone ignores X, and the tension must equal X’s mass times the common acceleration.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Two cars, initially next to each other and at rest, accelerate in the same straight line at different uniform rates. After 3 s, they are 12 m apart. If they continue to accelerate at the same rate, how far apart will they be 6 s after they started?
questions.stemText: Two cars, initially next to each other and at rest, accelerate in the same straight line at different uniform rates. After 3 s, they are 12 m apart. If they continue to accelerate at the same rate, how far apart will they be 6 s after they started? A 18 m B 24 m C 36 m D 48 m

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recognising that the separation grows with the square of time for two cars starting from rest.
questions.misconception: Assuming separation grows linearly with time

explanation.body: For cars starting from rest, $s=\tfrac12at^2$ and $s'=\tfrac12a't^2$. At $3\ \mathrm{s}$, $12=\tfrac12(9)(a'-a)$, giving $a'-a=\tfrac83\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. At $6\ \mathrm{s}$, the separation is $\tfrac12(36)(\tfrac83)=48\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the separation by treating the added time as a fixed increment instead of applying the square-time relation.
perOption.B: Doubles the separation as if it were proportional to time.
perOption.C: Triples the separation, though doubling the time multiplies it by four.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A parachutist falls from a stationary balloon at time $t=0$. The velocity–time graph for the parachutist from time $t=0$ until the time when he is just above the ground is shown.

[The velocity rises from zero with decreasing gradient until P, stays constant from P to Q, then drops steeply at Q and levels off at a smaller positive velocity at R, which stays constant through S.]

Which graph best shows the variation with time of the acceleration of the parachutist?

[All four acceleration–time graphs mark 0, P, Q, R and S. Acceleration is zero from P to Q and R to S in every option.]
A [Positive acceleration falls to zero by P. At Q it jumps to a negative value of about the initial magnitude and returns to zero by R.]
B [Positive acceleration falls to zero by P. At Q it jumps to a negative value much larger in magnitude than the initial acceleration and returns to zero by R.]
C [Negative acceleration rises to zero by P. At Q it jumps to a positive value of about the initial magnitude and returns to zero by R.]
D [Negative acceleration rises to zero by P. At Q it jumps to a positive value much larger in magnitude than the initial acceleration and returns to zero by R.]

stemImage.alt: Question 9: A parachutist falls from a stationary balloon at time t = 0. The velocity–time graph for the parachutist from time t = 0 until the time when he is just above th

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires comparing the signs and relative sizes of velocity gradients through four stages.
questions.misconception: Reading acceleration from the height of a velocity graph

explanation.body: From release to P, the positive velocity gradient falls from $g$ to zero. From P to Q, air resistance balances weight at the first terminal velocity, so acceleration is zero. When the parachute opens at Q, the steep negative gradient gives a negative acceleration with a magnitude much greater than $g$. The gradient returns to zero at R and stays there through S at the second terminal velocity.

perOption.A: Shows too small a negative acceleration at Q for the steep velocity gradient.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Reverses the signs of the velocity gradients before P and after Q.
perOption.D: Reverses the signs of both changing-velocity intervals, even though it shows a large spike at Q.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A block is moving along a horizontal frictionless surface. A constant force F and a constant resistive force of 5.0 N act on the block as it is moving in the direction of the force F, as shown.

The graph shows the variation with time of the momentum of the block.

What is the magnitude of F?
questions.stemText: A block is moving along a horizontal frictionless surface. A constant force F and a constant resistive force of 5.0 N act on the block as it is moving in the direction of the force F, as shown. The graph shows the variation with time of the momentum of the block. What is the magnitude of F? A 2.0 N B 3.0 N C 5.0 N D 8.0 N

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires reading the momentum gradient and using its sign in a force balance.
questions.misconception: Confusing resultant force with an individual force

explanation.body: The magnitude of the momentum–time gradient is $(2.7-1.5)/0.40=3.0\ \mathrm{N}$, giving the magnitude of the resultant force. Momentum decreases, so the resultant acts opposite to the motion. Thus $5.0-F=3.0$ and $F=2.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Takes the magnitude of the resultant as the applied force.
perOption.C: Assumes the applied and resistive forces balance despite the falling momentum.
perOption.D: Adds the resultant magnitude to the resistive force, giving a resultant in the direction of motion.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A man throws a ball vertically upwards. The ball travels $25\%$ of the total distance from the hand to the maximum height in the last second of its ascent.

What is the time of the ascent given that the effects due to air resistance are negligible?

A $1.25\ \mathrm{s}$
B $1.50\ \mathrm{s}$
C $1.67\ \mathrm{s}$
D $2.00\ \mathrm{s}$

stemImage.alt: Question 6: A man throws a ball vertically upwards. The ball travels 25 of the total distance from the hand to the maximum height in the last second of its ascent. What is

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires linking the last second and the whole ascent through their shared endpoint at zero speed.
questions.misconception: Assuming distance is proportional to time during the ascent

explanation.body: Let $h$ be the total rise and $v$ the speed at the start of the final second. Over that second, $0=v^2-2g(0.25h)$ and $0=\sqrt{0.50gh}-g(1)$, giving $h=19.62\ \mathrm{m}$. For the whole ascent, $0=u^2-2(9.81)(19.62)$ gives the launch speed $u=19.62\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The ascent time $T$ then follows from $0=19.62-9.81T$, so $T=2.00\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Adds 25% of a second to the final second, confusing a distance fraction with a time increment.
perOption.B: This time makes the final second cover about 44% of the rise, from the constant-acceleration distance relation.
perOption.C: This time makes the final second cover about 36% of the rise, from the constant-acceleration distance relation.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An elevator is moving upwards with an acceleration of 5.8 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. A ball, held 2.0 m above the floor of the elevator and at rest with respect to the elevator, is released.

How long does it take for the ball to reach the floor of the elevator?
questions.stemText: An elevator is moving upwards with an acceleration of 5.8 m s−2. A ball, held 2.0 m above the floor of the elevator and at rest with respect to the elevator, is released. How long does it take for the ball to reach the floor of the elevator? A 0.51 s B 0.64 s C 0.83 s D 1.0 s

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires finding the acceleration relative to the elevator before applying a standard motion equation.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the floor's acceleration

explanation.body: The ball accelerates downwards relative to the elevator at $9.81+5.8=15.61\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Its initial relative velocity is zero, so $s=ut+\frac12at^2$ gives $2.0=\frac12(15.61)t^2$. Thus $t=0.51\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the floor as unaccelerated and uses $g$ alone.
perOption.C: Uses the elevator's acceleration alone and omits the ball's downward acceleration.
perOption.D: Overestimates the time by underestimating how quickly the gap closes.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A mass of $0.40\ \mathrm{kg}$ moving along a smooth surface at $0.080\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ collides with the side of a vertical wall at an angle of $60^\circ$. The mass is in contact with the side of the wall for $0.20\ \mathrm{s}$. It bounces off at the same angle with the same speed. [A dashed horizontal line XY is perpendicular to the wall, with X to the left and Y to the right. The incoming path runs from the lower left towards the wall, and the outgoing path runs towards the upper left. Each path makes $60^\circ$ with the wall. The incoming arrow is labelled $0.080\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.] What is the magnitude of the average force the wall exerts on the ball along XY?
A $0.080\ \mathrm{N}$
B $0.14\ \mathrm{N}$
C $0.16\ \mathrm{N}$
D $0.28\ \mathrm{N}$

stemImage.alt: Question 4: A mass of 0.40 kg moving along a smooth surface at 0.080 m s−1 collides with the side of a vertical wall at an angle of 60. The mass is in contact with the sid

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must resolve the velocity perpendicular to the wall and account for its reversal.
questions.misconception: Omitting the reversal of the normal velocity

explanation.body: Along XY, the momentum changes by $0.40[0.080\sin 60^\circ-(-0.080\sin 60^\circ)]=0.0554\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, taking the rebound direction as positive. Dividing by the contact time gives an average force of $0.0554/0.20=0.28\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Uses the component parallel to the wall and counts only one momentum term.
perOption.B: Uses only the incoming normal momentum, as if the mass stopped along XY.
perOption.C: Uses the component parallel to the wall as the component that reverses.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An object is dropped at time $t=0$ s from a tall building. Air resistance is significant. Three graphs are plotted against time:

• the height of the object above the ground
• the speed of the object
• the magnitude of the resultant force on the object.

[Graph X starts at a positive value and falls steeply at first, flattening to zero. Graph Y starts at a positive value with a horizontal tangent, then falls with increasing steepness. Graph Z starts at zero, rises and levels off at a positive value. Each horizontal axis is labelled time.]

What are the quantities X, Y and Z?

Option | height of the object above the ground | speed of the object | magnitude of the resultant force on the object
A | X | Y | Z
B | X | Z | Y
C | Z | Y | X
D | Y | Z | X

stemImage.alt: Question 2: An object is dropped at time t = 0 s from a tall building. Air resistance is significant. Three graphs are plotted against time: • the height of the object abov

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Identifying the curves requires relating speed to the height gradient and drag to resultant force.
questions.misconception: Treating a falling height curve as a falling speed curve.

explanation.body: Y is height: it starts above zero with zero slope, and the magnitude of its slope increases to the constant terminal speed. Z is speed: it starts at zero and levels off at terminal speed. X is the resultant force: it starts at the weight because drag is initially zero, then falls to zero as drag rises to equal the weight.

perOption.A: Assigns Y to speed even though it starts above zero, and Z to force even though it starts at zero.
perOption.B: Uses X for height even though it starts with a steep slope, and Y for force even though it fails to fall to zero as Z levels off.
perOption.C: Uses Z for height even though it starts at zero, and Y for speed even though it starts above zero.
perOption.D: Correct. Height, speed and resultant force correspond to Y, Z and X respectively.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A person is suspended from a rope vertically below a helicopter.

The helicopter and the person are stationary above the ground. Which force forms a Newton's third law force pair with the weight of the person?
questions.stemText: A person is suspended from a rope vertically below a helicopter. The helicopter and the person are stationary above the ground. Which force forms a Newton's third law force pair with the weight of the person? A the force of tension in the rope on the person B the force of upthrust on the person C the gravitational force applied by the person on the Earth D the gravitational force applied by the person on the helicopter

options.label: A
options.text: the force of tension in the rope on the person

options.label: B
options.text: the force of upthrust on the person

options.label: C
options.text: the gravitational force applied by the person on the Earth

options.label: D
options.text: the gravitational force applied by the person on the helicopter

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires identifying the two bodies in one gravitational interaction.
questions.misconception: Confusing balanced forces with a third-law pair.

explanation.body: The person's weight is the gravitational force exerted by the Earth on the person. Its Newton's third-law partner is the gravitational force exerted by the person on the Earth.

perOption.A: Tension acts on the person and belongs to the rope–person interaction.
perOption.B: Upthrust acts on the person and belongs to the air–person interaction.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: This gravitational force pairs with the helicopter's pull on the person.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The water surface in a deep well is $78.0\ \mathrm{m}$ below the top of the well.
A person at the top of the well drops a heavy stone down the well.
Air resistance is negligible. The speed of sound in the air is $330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
What is the time interval between the person dropping the stone and hearing it hitting the water?

A $3.75\ \mathrm{s}$
B $3.99\ \mathrm{s}$
C $4.19\ \mathrm{s}$
D $4.22\ \mathrm{s}$

stemImage.alt: Question 5: The water surface in a deep well is 78.0 m below the top of the well. A person at the top of the well drops a heavy stone down the well. Air resistance is negli

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding and adding the times for two successive stages.
questions.misconception: Omitting the sound travel time.

explanation.body: For the falling stone, use $s=ut_1+\frac{1}{2}gt_1^2$ with zero initial speed to get $t_1=3.988\ \mathrm{s}$. The sound takes $t_2=78.0/330=0.236\ \mathrm{s}$ to travel back up the well. The total is $t_1+t_2=4.224\ \mathrm{s}$, which rounds to $4.22\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the sound travel time from the fall time.
perOption.B: Counts only the fall time.
perOption.C: Uses $g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, which gives a shorter fall time.
perOption.D: Correct.
